raw_text:
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. For decades, the transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has served as the gold standard for SCD prevention. However, transvenous leads are vulnerable to mechanical stress, resulting in fractures, insulation failures, and venous thrombosis. Furthermore, lead-related systemic infections often progress to endocarditis, requiring high-risk transvenous lead extraction. To circumvent these intravascular complications, the entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed, avoiding the heart and vasculature completely [1, 2].

The S-ICD system consists of a pulse generator placed in a left lateral thoracic pocket and a subcutaneous lead positioned parasternally [1]. Because the S-ICD relies on far-field electrocardiogram (ECG) signals rather than near-field intracardiac electrograms, pre-implantation ECG screening is mandatory to prevent T-wave oversensing (TWO) and subsequent inappropriate shocks [3, 4]. This screening process, originally manual and now automated, evaluates specific sensing vectors across different body postures to confirm acceptable QRS-to-T-wave ratios [4]. During the surgical procedure, appropriate anesthetic management is critical to ensure patient comfort and facilitate defibrillation threshold testing if required [5].

The clinical safety and efficacy of the S-ICD were initially established through several large registries and observational cohorts. The international EFFORTLESS registry [6, 7] and the S-ICD Post-Approval Study (PAS) [8] demonstrated high rates of successful arrhythmia conversion and low rates of early device-related complications [9, 10, 11]. Long-term follow-up data from these cohorts confirmed that the clinical benefits of the S-ICD are sustained over time [12, 13].

Crucially, the landmark PRAETORIAN trial—the first randomized controlled trial directly comparing S-ICD and TV-ICD therapies—demonstrated that the S-ICD was non-inferior to the TV-ICD regarding the primary composite endpoint of inappropriate shocks and device-related complications [14]. While S-ICD patients had fewer lead-related complications, they experienced slightly higher rates of inappropriate shocks, though this difference did not reach statistical significance [14]. To address this, the UNTOUCHED trial evaluated S-ICD performance in a primary prevention population with low ejection fractions, demonstrating that standardized programming and contemporary filters could reduce inappropriate shocks to rates lower than those historically reported for TV-ICDs [15].

Despite the benefits of avoiding transvenous leads, inappropriate shocks historically remained a key limitation of S-ICD therapy [16, 17]. These events are mostly driven by TWO or non-cardiac noise oversensing. To mitigate this issue, advanced sensing algorithms were developed [18]. The clinical introduction of the SMART Pass 2-Hz high-pass filter significantly reduced inappropriate shock rates by suppressing low-frequency T-waves without compromising ventricular fibrillation detection [19, 20]. Implantation techniques have also evolved; the transition from a three-incision technique to a two-incision technique [21], and the adoption of the intermuscular pocket (placing the generator between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles) [22], have reduced complication rates, shortened procedural times, and improved cosmetic outcomes.

The S-ICD is highly advantageous for young patients, those with limited vascular access, high infection risk (such as patients on hemodialysis), and patients with channelopathies like Brugada syndrome [23] or structural disorders like hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [24]. Reflecting this clinical evidence, major international guidelines from the AHA/ACC/HRS [25] and the ESC [26, 27, 28] recommend the S-ICD as a Class I or Class IIa alternative to TV-ICDs for patients who do not require pacing therapy for bradycardia, cardiac resynchronization, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP).

The principal limitation of the S-ICD remains its lack of chronic pacing and ATP capabilities [20]. To address this gap, modular cardiac rhythm management systems have been developed [29, 30]. This system combines the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker (LCP) implanted in the right ventricle. The S-ICD and LCP communicate wirelessly to provide demand pacing and ATP, preserving the extravascular nature of the S-ICD while adding pacing functionality [30].

In conclusion, the S-ICD is a mature and highly effective alternative to transvenous systems, offering a robust solution to lead-related and systemic infectious complications. Continued algorithm refinement and the clinical integration of modular leadless pacing systems will continue to expand its utility, making it an increasingly preferred option for sudden cardiac death prevention.
